UNDERSTANDING AWS AMPLIFY & WHY IT’S PERFECT FOR PERSONAL PROJECTS / STUDENT ASSIGNMENTS Every time you work on a student assignment or build a personal project, you’ve probably faced this scenario: finishing the Frontend is quick, but building the Backend, configuring the Database, integrating Sign-up/Sign-in, and deploying to a server takes a lot of time. To solve the problem of complex infrastructure setup and help you focus entirely on application logic, AWS Amplify is a solution worth considering.
Key points to know:
What it is: AWS Amplify is a set of tools and services that help developers build full-stack Web and Mobile applications quickly on AWS infrastructure without needing deep Cloud or DevOps management expertise. Authentication: Integrates Amazon Cognito with just a few CLI commands or simple configuration steps. It provides ready-made flows for sign-up, sign-in, password recovery, and secure session management. API & Database: Flexibly initialize GraphQL APIs (AWS AppSync) or REST APIs (API Gateway combined with DynamoDB). Data operations from the Frontend are optimized and synced smoothly. Hosting & Automated CI/CD: Connects directly to GitHub or GitLab. Every time you push new code (git push), the system automatically handles the Build and Deploy processes. Pros: Optimal deployment speed (especially suitable for demos, coursework, or MVPs), Serverless architecture saves costs and server management effort, and excellent multi-platform support (React, Next.js, Vue, Flutter, React Native, etc.). Cons: When the application scales and requires deep infrastructure customization (like configuring a private VPC or complex IAM permissions), intervening in resources automatically created by Amplify will require additional research time. This solution is particularly useful when you want to optimize the development process, deploy your product to the Cloud professionally, and save time, rather than struggling with manual infrastructure configurations.

title: Introduction
content:
Concepts RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve relevant text first (Retrieval), add it to the prompt (Augmentation), then let the model answer from that text only (Generation). Knowledge base on DynamoDB: legal articles are stored as items in a DynamoDB table and found by keyword. It is simple and fits the AWS Free Tier, but it does not understand meaning the way vector search does. Serverless: Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB scale automatically and charge by usage, which fits a low-budget project. Groq API: an external inference service that runs the language model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b) and is called from Lambda over HTTPS. Problem and goals Employees need fast answers about personal-data rules (for example, using customers’ ID card data for advertising). A public chatbot may invent articles or citations. Goal: answers grounded only in the legal text the team provided, running at near-zero cost on AWS.
Architecture and data flow Data flow The user opens the website on S3, types a question in the chat box and sends it. index.html sends an HTTPS POST request to API Gateway. API Gateway checks CORS and forwards the payload to the Lambda function. Lambda queries the DynamoDB table LegalArticles for articles related to the question (function retrieve_legal_context). DynamoDB returns the matching articles to Lambda as legal context. Lambda builds a complete prompt (system prompt + legal context + question) and calls the Groq API. Groq returns the generated text answer to Lambda. Lambda formats the standard JSON response (with error codes if needed) and returns it to API Gateway. API Gateway returns the result and the chat box displays it. Lambda logs go to Amazon CloudWatch throughout. Components Component AWS service / resource Prompt & RAG logic Lambda (Python) Knowledge base DynamoDB – LegalArticles Backend API API Gateway + Lambda Frontend S3 static website – index.html Security & operations CloudWatch, Budgets, IAM Implemented vs. planned The system differs from the first design in several places. This table keeps the workshop honest about what exists today.
Area First design Implemented now Knowledge base S3 + Bedrock Knowledge Bases DynamoDB table LegalArticles (keyword lookup) LLM Amazon Bedrock Groq API (external, outside AWS) Frontend AWS Amplify S3 static website Authentication Cognito None yet (public API) Response format Structured: risk level, provisions, evidence… Text answer wrapped in JSON Conversation history DynamoDB Not implemented Incident report + alert SNS Future work AI safety principles Preliminary assessment only, never an official legal conclusion. Answer only from the provided legal articles; never invent provisions or citations. No basis in the database → say so explicitly.

content:
WHAT NEW AWS LEARNERS NEED TO KNOW TO AVOID END-OF-MONTH BILL SHOCK One of the most common scenarios for AWS beginners is accidentally leaving a test resource running and forgetting to turn it off, only to receive an unexpected bill at the end of the month. Controlling costs not only gives you peace of mind while practicing but is also a fundamental skill in cloud infrastructure management.
Key points to know:
Set up AWS Budgets & Billing Alerts: Configure a safe budget threshold (e.g., $5 or $10). The system will automatically send an email alert when actual or forecasted costs exceed this limit, helping you catch hidden running resources early. Utilize the AWS Free Tier correctly: Understand the specific conditions. For example, EC2 offers 750 hours/month for t2.micro or t3.micro instances. Running two instances simultaneously will double the usage and quickly exceed the free limit. Always check the storage and request limits for S3 and EBS. Clean up unused resources: Stop or delete EC2 instances when not in use. Note that Elastic IPs are only free when attached to a Running instance; you will still be charged if they are unattached or attached to a Stopped instance. Also, remember to delete unattached EBS volumes and snapshots to avoid hidden storage fees. Track details with AWS Cost Explorer: Use this visual tool to analyze costs over time, by service, or by Tag. Checking the cost report 1-2 times a week helps you quickly spot any unusual spending patterns. Cost optimization and control are essential parts of the cloud computing mindset. Setting up a safe infrastructure from the start allows you to learn and experiment with AWS services completely worry-free.

title: Blog 3
content:
BUILDING A SIMPLE, SECURE STATIC WEBSITE WITH S3 + CLOUDFRONT + ROUTE 53 When you finish a static website (pure HTML/CSS/JS or builds from React, Vue, Next.js), the next challenge is choosing a storage and distribution solution for the internet. The typical goals are: optimized costs, fast access speed, secure HTTPS support, and zero server management effort. The trio of Amazon S3 + Amazon CloudFront + Route 53 is the standardized architecture that solves this problem optimally.
Key points to know:
Step 1: File Storage with Amazon S3: Create an S3 Bucket to hold the built static web source code. Configure the S3 Bucket Policy with appropriate access rights and enable Static website hosting to set default access files (e.g., index.html and 404.html). Step 2: Acceleration & Security with Amazon CloudFront (CDN): Create a CloudFront Distribution and point the Origin to the newly created S3 Bucket. Data is cached at global Edge Locations to minimize latency. Integrate a free SSL/TLS certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to enable HTTPS. Configure Origin Access Control (OAC) to block direct external access to the S3 Bucket, allowing traffic only through CloudFront. Step 3: Domain Routing with Amazon Route 53: Create a Hosted Zone for your custom domain on Route 53. Configure an A Record (Alias) to point the main domain or subdomain to the CloudFront Distribution address. Technical Value: Cost optimization (fully Serverless, monthly costs are near $0 for small projects), Scalability (CloudFront’s CDN network automatically handles traffic spikes without infrastructure upgrades), and simplified operations (no need to worry about OS patching or periodic SSL certificate management). This is one of the classic yet highly important hands-on practices, helping you master the mindset of combining fundamental AWS services to create a complete, secure, and industry-standard system.

title: Worklog
Proposal
content:
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the project that you plan to conduct.
Automated Legal RAG Platform (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP) A Serverless LLM Solution for Real-Time Legal Data Retrieval and Analysis 1. Executive Summary The Automated Legal RAG Platform is designed to assist users and team members in quickly retrieving and analyzing complex legal regulations in Vietnam, specifically focusing on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection. The platform leverages a comprehensive Serverless architecture on AWS combined with a powerful Large Language Model via Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). This solution delivers highly accurate, context-aware queries, eliminating AI hallucination, while minimizing operational costs to nearly $0 by fully utilizing the AWS Free Tier.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Legal documents such as Decree 13/2023/ND-CP are lengthy, dry, and difficult for non-experts to manually navigate and search. Standard general-purpose AI tools (like the free tier of ChatGPT) often lack deep knowledge of Vietnamese law and tend to provide vague answers without an accurate legal basis. Furthermore, building a self-hosted AI system is typically hardware-intensive and requires complex server management.
The Solution Implement an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline: When a user asks a question, the system scans the database to retrieve the most accurate legal clauses and injects them into the System Prompt. The LLM then processes this information to deliver an answer with clear legal citations. The platform utilizes Amazon DynamoDB to store extracted legal clauses (LegalArticles), AWS Lambda for backend RAG logic processing combined with Amazon API Gateway for a stable API Endpoint, Groq API with the qwen/qwen3.8-27b model for intelligent natural language generation, and an Amazon S3 Static Website for intuitive user interaction.
Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) The solution guarantees high accuracy by strictly following provided legal context, ensuring transparency and valid grounding. It achieves extreme cost optimization by operating entirely on a Serverless model, maximizing the AWS Free Tier to keep monthly maintenance costs at $0. Additionally, the decoupled architecture ensures high scalability, allowing for the easy addition of new legal frameworks (e.g., Cybersecurity Law, IT Law) to DynamoDB in the future.
3. Solution Architecture The system employs a Serverless architecture, seamlessly connecting the Frontend, Backend, and external LLM. Data flows from the user interface through the API Gateway to the Lambda function, which retrieves context from DynamoDB and queries the Groq API. The architecture is detailed below:
(Placeholder for Architecture Diagram: S3 Static Website -> API Gateway -> AWS Lambda (RAG Logic) -> Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles) & Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b))
AWS Services & Technologies Used
Amazon S3 Static Website: Stores and serves the static website interface (index.html, CSS, JS) to users. Amazon API Gateway: Provides a public HTTP/REST API, handles CORS, and acts as the entry point for client requests to Lambda. AWS Lambda (Python): Executes the backend source code to process RAG logic, retrieve data from DynamoDB, and interact with the Groq API. Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles): Stores the structure of legal clauses, supporting high-speed keyword queries. Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b): Synthesizes and analyzes natural language based on the injected legal context. Component Design
User Interface (Frontend): Users access the website from S3 and type questions into the chat box. The browser sends an HTTPS POST Request containing the question to the API Gateway. Gateway (API Gateway): Receives the request, checks CORS security headers, and forwards the data payload to the Lambda function. Data Retrieval (DynamoDB): Lambda executes the retrieve_legal_context function to scan and search for relevant clauses in the LegalArticles table (e.g., penalty regulations related to Citizen ID cards and personal data). Augmentation & Generation (Groq API): Lambda packages the user’s question along with the retrieved legal context into a strictly constrained System Prompt, then calls the Groq API. Response Flow: Groq returns the result to Lambda, which formats the data into a standard JSON structure and sends it back via API Gateway to be displayed on the user’s chat interface. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project follows a structured 3-phase development cycle:
Phase 1: Prompt Setup & RAG Mechanism: Build the System Prompt defining the AI’s role as a legal expert and establish Context Constraints to absolutely prevent information fabrication (hallucination). Phase 2: Backend & Database Deployment: Create the DynamoDB table LegalArticles. Write Python code on AWS Lambda integrating data retrieval functions and Groq API calls. Configure API Gateway, enable CORS Headers, and build standardized error handling (returning code 400 for invalid data, 502/504 for system errors, and handling code 429 for Groq API rate limits). Phase 3: Testing & Refinement: Use the curl command to send test HTTP POST requests or test directly on the web interface, and verify logs on Amazon CloudWatch. Technical Requirements
Backend Engine: Python for AWS Lambda, boto3 for DynamoDB and AWS service integration, and HTTP clients for Groq API calls. Database Schema: DynamoDB LegalArticles table optimized for high-speed keyword queries and context retrieval. Prompt Engineering: Strictly constrained System Prompt enforcing responses based only on the provided DynamoDB context. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Week 1: Research & Design phase. Define the legal scope (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP), design the RAG data flow, and draft the System Prompt. Week 2: Development & Deployment phase. Build the DynamoDB database, complete the Lambda function, configure the API Gateway, and set up the S3 static website. Week 3: Integration & Testing phase. Connect the frontend with the API Gateway, test the accuracy of answers from the Groq LLM, optimize error handling, and finalize documentation. 6. Budget Estimation The architecture is strictly optimized to operate at $0 monthly cost by fully utilizing free tiers.
Amazon S3: $0.00/month (Within Free Tier limits for static website hosting). Amazon API Gateway: $0.00/month (Free for the first 1 million requests/month). AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (Free for the first 1 million requests/month). Amazon DynamoDB: $0.00/month (Free for 25GB storage, 25 WCU / 25 RCU). Groq API: $0.00/month (Free tier utilized for the open-source model qwen/qwen3.8-27b). Total Project Investment: $0.00 (0 VNĐ) / month. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix
API Overload (Rate Limit 429 from Groq API): Medium impact, medium probability. AI Hallucination: High impact, medium probability (mitigated). Browser CORS Errors: High impact, low probability (mitigated). Mitigation Strategies
API Overload: Implement robust Error Handling mechanisms and display friendly notification messages on the chat interface when the system temporarily exceeds call frequency limits. AI Hallucination: Tighten the System Prompt with strict rules requiring the use of only the legal context provided by DynamoDB, strictly forbidding external deduction or fabrication. CORS Errors: Fully configure CORS Headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, POST, OPTIONS) directly within the API Gateway settings to ensure seamless browser-to-backend communication. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements:
Successfully deploy a complete, auto-scaling, and stable Serverless Backend. Optimize operational costs to an absolute minimum ($0) through strategic use of AWS Free Tier and Groq’s free tier. Eliminate AI hallucinations via strict RAG context injection and constrained System Prompts. Long-term Value:
Provide a standardized API endpoint and an intuitive chat interface to quickly and accurately query core regulations within Decree 13/2023/ND-CP. Effectively serve academic research and practical study needs. Create a highly scalable foundation that allows for the seamless integration of additional legal frameworks (e.g., Cybersecurity Law, IT Law) in the future.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Event Objectives Explore how the rise of generative AI is reshaping the daily responsibilities and long-term value of software engineers. Unpack foundational AWS design philosophies around scalability, resilience, and operational discipline. Define the evolving skill set required to thrive as a modern engineer (the “Renaissance Developer”). Establish a realistic perspective on AI as a productivity multiplier rather than a replacement for human expertise. Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer and Vice President, Amazon & AWS Key Highlights Scaling Pains and the Birth of Custom Infrastructure The Breaking Point: A massive holiday-season database crash at early Amazon resulted in a full day of downtime and severe financial impact. The Discovery: A deep dive into traffic patterns revealed that the vast majority of database calls were trivial key-value lookups, not complex relational queries. The Innovation: Instead of forcing a generic enterprise database to handle hyper-scale workloads, Amazon engineered its own distributed key-value system, laying the groundwork for Dynamo and DynamoDB. Core Lesson: At massive scale, off-the-shelf tools often become bottlenecks. True innovation sometimes requires building bespoke solutions tailored to your specific access patterns. Core Principles of Reliable Systems Focus on the Tail End: Average latency metrics hide poor user experiences. Engineering teams must optimize for the 99.9th percentile (P99.9) to guarantee consistent performance. Assume Inevitable Failure: Architectures must be built with the baseline assumption that hardware, networks, and data centers will fail, and the system must survive gracefully. Proactive Chaos Testing: “GameDays” are mandatory drills where production environments are intentionally disrupted to validate automated failover and recovery processes without human intervention. Customer-Aligned Economics: The shift to pay-as-you-go cloud models forces providers to continuously prove their value, aligning vendor success directly with customer reliability. The “Renaissance Developer” Profile Relentless Curiosity: Treating the rapid evolution of frameworks and languages as an opportunity for lifelong learning, not a burden. Holistic Systems View: Zooming out from isolated code modules to understand how data and services flow across the entire ecosystem. Ultimate Accountability: AI might draft the code, but the human engineer remains fully accountable for security flaws, production outages, and architectural soundness. T-Shaped Competency: Combining deep expertise in a primary domain with functional literacy in adjacent areas (e.g., frontend, data modeling, business logic). Strategic Communication: Translating technical trade-offs into business terms, ensuring that engineering decisions solve actual business problems rather than just chasing trends. The Human-AI Dynamic AI as a Force Multiplier: Generative AI acts like a highly productive but imperfect compiler. It drastically shrinks prototyping time but cannot be trusted blindly. The Irreplaceable Human Element: Critical thinking, ethical judgment, creative problem-solving, and an understanding of edge cases remain strictly human domains. A Warning on Stagnation: Echoing Grace Hopper, the greatest risk to a tech career is the comfort of “We’ve always done it this way.” Key Takeaways Strategic Mindset Own the Outcome: Delegation to AI does not mean delegation of responsibility. Question Legacy Habits: Regularly audit existing processes to ensure they aren’t just artifacts of past limitations. Think in Systems: Optimize the entire value stream, not just individual components. Architectural Discipline Measure the Worst-Case: Shift monitoring dashboards to highlight P99/P99.9 latency to uncover hidden friction. Automate Resilience: Recovery from failure should be a programmed response, not a manual scramble. Right-Size the Tech: Match the database and compute technology to the actual shape of the workload, not the other way around. Career & Team Strategy Broaden Your Horizons: Encourage cross-training within the team to build T-shaped skill sets. Use AI for Drafting, Humans for Review: Leverage AI for boilerplate and initial scaffolding, but enforce strict human-led reviews for security and logic. Applying to Work Initiate a “GameDay”: Propose a controlled failure simulation for our current staging environment to test our alerting and auto-recovery mechanisms. Audit Monitoring Dashboards: Review our current observability setup and add P99.9 latency tracking for our most critical user journeys. Re-evaluate Database Usage: Analyze our current data access patterns to see if any heavy relational workloads could be optimized with a simpler key-value or document store. Facilitate Cross-Team Syncs: Organize brief knowledge-sharing sessions where engineers explain technical constraints to product managers, fostering a shared vocabulary. Standardize AI-Assisted Reviews: Update our PR guidelines to explicitly require human validation of AI-generated code, focusing on edge cases and security implications. Event Experience Attending Dr. Werner Vogels’ keynote was a refreshing and grounding experience. Rather than hyping AI as a magic bullet, the session provided a mature, historically grounded perspective on how technology evolves and how engineers must evolve with it.
Insights from a Industry Veteran Hearing the firsthand account of Amazon’s early database struggles made the concept of “building vs. buying” much more tangible. It highlighted that true architectural breakthroughs often come from deeply understanding your own unique constraints. The emphasis on operational excellence reinforced that reliability is not an afterthought; it is a deliberate, continuously practiced discipline. Conceptual Takeaways The P99.9 latency concept was a major “aha” moment. It completely shifts how I view performance metrics, moving the focus from “mostly working” to “consistently working for everyone.” The GameDay methodology provides a concrete, actionable framework for building confidence in our system’s resilience, rather than just hoping it holds up under pressure. Reframing the AI Narrative The session directly addressed my own underlying anxieties about AI automation. Framing AI as an “imprecise compiler” was a brilliant analogy. It clarified that my value as an engineer isn’t in typing syntax, but in applying judgment, context, and accountability to the output. Networking and Broader Perspective Discussions with peers after the talk highlighted a shared desire to bridge the gap between engineering and business units. The “Renaissance Developer” model gives us a clear target for the soft skills and cross-functional knowledge we need to cultivate. Personal Lessons Learned Complacency is the real enemy, not AI. Sticking to legacy patterns because they are comfortable is a greater career risk than adopting new tools. Resilience must be engineered and tested, not assumed. The most powerful tool in an engineer’s arsenal remains their ability to communicate complex trade-offs clearly to non-technical stakeholders. Some event photos Ultimately, this about enduring engineering principles. It left me feeling empowered to take greater ownership of my systems, leverage AI thoughtfully, and continuously challenge the status quo in my daily work.

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “AWS First Cloud Journey AI - Technical Deep Dives” Event Objectives Explore building Vietnamese voice-AI contact centers on AWS using cascade and duplex architectures. Understand AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for secure, multi-account resource sharing and landing zone design. Learn about securing web applications with AI-powered autonomous security agents. Introduce Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime and memory architecture. Speakers Kiet Tran – AI Engineer, Revve AI Thinh Nguyen – DevSecOps/Cloud Engineer Xuan An – Leader, AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE Key Highlights Building a Vietnamese Voice-AI Contact Center (Revve AI) The Problem: Contact centers face traffic peaks, repetitive tasks, and limited QA sampling. Human turn-taking gap is ~200ms. Three Architectures: Cascade (ASR → LLM → TTS): Text in the middle acts as a checkpoint. Strong control/guardrails, best for Vietnamese (production today). Speech-to-Speech (S2S): One model, audio in → audio out (e.g., Nova 2 Sonic). Lower latency, keeps tone, but limited Vietnamese support. Full Duplex S2S: Two streams always open (e.g., Gemini Live). Lowest latency, backchanneling, but weakest control and mostly English-only. Revve on AWS Architecture: One region, inside customer’s account. Uses EKS, GPU nodes (G6/L4) for speech, and Bedrock via PrivateLink for LLM. Bank POC Results: 799 test calls, 93% intent match on 871 labelled turns, 35/35 outbound outcomes classified right. Four Lessons Paid For: Benchmark turn detection in your own language (Vietnamese vs English padding mismatch). Normalize numbers before TTS (e.g., “500K” → “ca”). Use a small judge model to check sentences before TTS to prevent bad output. Latency budget picks the model (Self-hosted Gemma: 0.24s vs Hosted: 1.15-1.95s). AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) Fundamentals The Multi-Account Challenge: Without sharing, resources (Transit GW, DNS rules) are duplicated in every account, leading to drift and high costs. AWS RAM allows creating once and sharing everywhere. Core Concepts: A resource share is a Regional container holding Resources (ARNs), Managed Permissions (what consumers can do), and Principals (who gets access: accounts, OUs, org). Deep Dive: RAM is Regional; global resources (like Cloud WAN) are shared from us-east-1 only. AZ names are mapped randomly per account; always use AZ IDs (e.g., use1-az4) in IaC for shared subnets. Enterprise Blueprint: Management account enables org sharing. Infrastructure and Security OUs share resources (Subnets, TGW, Firewall policies) to the Workloads OU (Prod/Non-prod/Data & AI) automatically via membership. Operations: Monitor with EventBridge (alert on external principals) and CloudTrail (source of truth). Manage as code using CloudFormation or Terraform. Securing Web Apps with AWS Security Agent The Security Bottleneck: Manual pentests are time-consuming (weeks), expensive ($5k-$20k/engagement), and inconsistent. The Frontier Agent: Powered by Amazon Bedrock. Features autonomous reasoning, full lifecycle coverage (Design Review → Code Security → Active Pentesting), and verifiable findings (attempts real exploitation). Capabilities: Design Review: Upload Markdown/Terraform, verify against Managed Packs (PCI DSS, NIST CSF). Free Tier: 200 reviews/month. Code Review: Integrated into GitHub/GitLab PRs, comments on code, suggests auto-fixes. Free Tier: 1,000 PR reviews/month. Automated Pentesting: Multi-step exploit chains (IDOR → XSS), authenticates like a real user, provides attack graphs. Pricing: $50 per Task-Hour (pay-as-you-go). Real-world case study: $1,500 - $2,500 total cost vs $10,000 for a pentest team. Critical Limitations: Auth blocks (MFA, Biometrics, mTLS stop the agent), difficulty detecting business-logic fraud without deep context, and task-hour accumulation in complex apps. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Introduction: AWS Bedrock AgentCore Unpacked: Master Class on Runtime and Memory Architecture. (Note: Only title slide provided) Key Takeaways Voice AI Strategy Control vs. Naturalness: For enterprise/banking in Vietnamese, the Cascade architecture is the only production-ready choice due to the need for text-based guardrails and language support. Duplex is on the horizon for pilots. Latency Budget: The choice of LLM (self-hosted vs. hosted) is dictated by the acceptable latency budget. Multi-Account Architecture Share, don’t duplicate: Use AWS RAM to maintain one resource, one owner, and one policy set. Lean on Organizations: Use OU-targeted, invitation-free, membership-driven access for automated scaling. Least Privilege: Layer RAM managed permissions with consumer IAM policies and SCPs. AI in Security Shift Left: AI agents can perform design and code reviews early in the SDLC, significantly reducing the cost and time of security audits. Verifiable Findings: Unlike standard LLM chatbots, security agents that attempt real exploitation provide proof of vulnerability. Applying to Work Voice AI: Evaluate cascade architectures for customer service automation, ensuring Vietnamese STT/TTS models are benchmarked locally. Cloud Infrastructure: Implement AWS RAM for shared VPCs, Transit Gateways, and DNS rules across development and production accounts. Pin shared subnets to AZ IDs in Terraform/CloudFormation. DevSecOps: Integrate AI security agents into GitHub/GitLab workflows for automated PR reviews and design verification against compliance frameworks. Agent Development: Explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for building advanced AI agents with persistent memory and runtime management. Event Experience Attending the AWS First Cloud Journey AI event was extremely valuable, providing a comprehensive view of how AI and modern cloud architectures are solving real-world enterprise problems. Key experiences included:
Learning from industry practitioners Kiet Tran shared hard-won lessons from deploying Vietnamese voice AI in a top-tier bank, highlighting the importance of language-specific benchmarking and the trade-offs between cascade and duplex models. Thinh Nguyen demonstrated how AI is transforming the security landscape, moving from manual, expensive pentests to autonomous, verifiable agent-based testing. Deep technical architecture insights The AWS RAM session provided a clear blueprint for enterprise landing zones, emphasizing the critical detail of using AZ IDs instead of AZ names for cross-account subnet sharing. The Revve on AWS architecture diagram illustrated a practical, secure deployment model using PrivateLink for Bedrock and GPU nodes for speech processing within the customer’s own account. Practical takeaways Learned that latency budgets dictate model selection in voice AI; a 0.24s self-hosted model is vastly different from a 1.95s hosted model in a conversational context. Understood the defense-in-depth approach in AWS RAM, where consumer IAM and SCPs still apply on top of the shared resource permissions. Recognized the limitations of AI security agents, particularly their inability to bypass MFA or understand deep business logic, reinforcing the need for human oversight in complex scenarios. Some event photos Overall, the event provided a dense, technical deep dive into cutting-edge AWS services, from voice AI and resource sharing to autonomous security agents, reshaping my understanding of how to build secure, scalable, and intelligent systems on the cloud.
